The deficiencies of price-taking price- responsive dispatch can occur at high levels of participation (not generally seen currently for EVMC) because price-responsive mechanisms are based on the assumption that the participating load is not large enough to significantly impact generator dispatch decisions. There is evidence in the literature that price-responsive mechanisms can provide savings even if they are large enough to affect generator dispatch decisions and that there is a breaking point beyond which price- responsive mechanisms increase, rather than decrease, power system costs (Xi and Sioshansi 2014; Muratori and Rizzoni 2016; Mahmud, Ravishankar, and Hossain 2020). This breaking point can also be thought of as the EVMC participation level at which price-making dispatch mechanisms (in our modeling, DLC) are preferred to price-taking dispatch mechanisms (TOU and real-time price, RTP). This study quantifies how improved forecasting of EVMC price-responsive dispatch increases the effectiveness and performance of TOU and RTP relative to DLC at higher participation rates. Our previous work (Hale et al. 2022a) pessimistically fixed the day-ahead unit commitment decisions used to estimate production costs with TOU and RTP EVMC based on the unmanaged EV charging profile, an assumption we refer to in this study as a “no-foresight forecast.” The no- foresight forecast resulted in TOU and RTP EVMC increasing production costs at participation rates beyond 2% to 14% of LDVs. However, this assumption is unrealistically pessimistic, especially for TOU rates that are in place for years—the responses to those rates are easily observed and incorporated into day-ahead load forecasts. In this study, we therefore bound the possible effectiveness of price-responsive dispatch mechanisms by also simulating day-ahead unit commitment decisions using EV charging profiles that incorporate the effects of optimally scheduling all participating vehicles’ charging based on TOU or RTP, which we refer to as the perfect-foresight forecast. We evaluate up to 45% of LDVs (100% of modeled EVs) participating in EVMC with both price- responsive (i.e., TOU, RTP) and DLC dispatch mechanisms in a realistic, low-carbon bulk power system simulated using a commercial production cost model, PLEXOS (Energy Exemplar). Previous research has often focused on coordinating flexible loads on smaller or synthetic systems (Cutler et al. 2021; Dall’Anese et al. 2018), modeled aggregate EVMC without ensuring that aggregate dispatch requests could be fulfilled by individual participating vehicles (Pertl et al. 2019; Szinai et al. 2020), or scheduled EV charging only within a day (Liu et al. 2012; Wood et al. 2017; Wood et al. 2023).
